nodes.label: idempotent
nodes.rationale: At-most-once write processing keyed by a client-supplied Idempotency-Key header: the handler runs only on the first request and later ones replay the stored response. A returned 4xx/5xx is cached unconditionally so a 'payment failed' reply is not re-processed into a success; a handler that throws drops its in-flight claim so the client can retry.

nodes.label: Request fingerprint
nodes.rationale: A SHA-256 fingerprint of method, path, query and body is stored alongside each cached response; a second request reusing the key with any of those differing is refused with 422, so a client cannot reuse a key for a semantically different request and receive the wrong stored response. Query keys are folded in canonically (sorted) so a reordered retry still replays, while a repeated key's values keep their order because some APIs read such a list positionally.

nodes.label: Idempotency key validation
nodes.rationale: The header value is attacker-chosen and lands verbatim in a cache key, so a key longer than maxKeyLength (255, Stripe's cap) or containing an ASCII control character or space is refused with 400 - CR/LF are the classic header-injection pair and space plus the control range are Memcached text-protocol delimiters. The rejection names the limit and the offending index, never the key itself, because echoing attacker bytes back is how a rejection message becomes a payload. This bounds how much cache one key costs, not how many a caller can mint.

nodes.label: In-flight 409 Conflict
nodes.rationale: A concurrent second request for the same key is rejected immediately with 409 rather than queued. Failing fast instead of holding the connection open for the handler's whole runtime also means there is no cross-pod lock to coordinate - the in-flight marker lives in the same cache as the cached responses.

nodes.label: Dedicated cache instance for idempotency
nodes.rationale: Every request can mint a new key and InMemoryCache is LRU-bounded with eviction blind to what an entry protects, so sharing an instance with rateLimit or cached lets a key flood through either push stored responses out - an honest retry then re-claims the key and runs the handler again, a double charge. Worse, setIfAbsent does not mark a record most-recently-used, so a claimed key nobody has retried ages toward eviction from the moment it is stored. Use a dedicated instance, or Redis where the guarantee must hold under an adversary.
